2. On these pleadings the parties fought out the suit. The court of first instance on a consideration of the evidence on record both oral and documentary came to the view that the defendant No. 1 had the onus to prove that the plaintiff was not the grand-son of Gour Majhi and he having failed to prove so the plaintiff would be considered to have proved that he was the son of Gour Majhi and that being the position the plaintiff would be a co-sharer of the suit land and therefore would be entitled to partition, holding further that the absence of the name of the plaintiff in the rent receipts, S A. Khatian and land acquisition case records, would not prove that the plaintiff was not a co-sharer and would not deprive the plaintiff from his share in the suit land. In that view of the matter the suit was decreed on contest without costs, in preliminary form. On appeal the said judgment was reversed by the learned Additional District Judge, on a finding that the court of first instance erred in law in shifting the onus upon the defendant to prove that the plaintiff was not the grand-son of Gour Majhi and allowed the appeal on a finding that the plaintiff was never the grand-son of Gour Majhi, but was the grand-son of ptoly Majhi, brother of Gour Majhi and thus had no interest and was not a co-sharer in the partible land and as such he could claim 8 annas share thereof on partition. In that view of the matter, the impugned judgment and decree of the learned Munsif were set aside and the original title suit bearing No. 171 of 1969 was dismissed. As against that the plaintiff has preferred this appeal to this court. 

 7. It was next contended by Mr. Fazlul Karim that the court of appeal below erred in taking into consideration the exhibits in considering the question of pedigree as they were not relevant to prove any family conduct within the meaning of Section 50 of the Evidence Act. The information gathered from the entry in S.A. Khatian, the L.A. case records and the rent receipts were not opinions of persons who had special means of knowledge in proving relationship. I do not find much substance in that contention. Under section 50 of the Evidence Act, opinion, belief or judgment of a person, having special means of knowledge as members of the family or otherwise of the relationship between two persons are relevant. Under section 144 of the Evidence Act, a court may presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to happen regard been had to the common course of natural events and human conduct. Section 50, read with section 114 of the Evidence Act would make the conduct of the members of a family, evidenced by the acceptance of the members of the family, the devolution and distribution of the family property amongst its, members, a very valuable evidence of family conduct, as contemplated under section 50 of the Evidence Act. In the instant case it is seen that the partible land in suit stood in the S.A. khatian solely in .the name of defendant No. 1 without its being objected to by the plaintiff at any point of time. If the plaintiff was the co-owner or a' co-sharer of the property left by Gour Majhi he would have made some attempt to rectify the mistakes in recording the co-sharer property in the khatian in the sole name of defendant No. 1. It. is further seen that in the Tahsil office the jama in respect of the partible land also stood in the name of defendant No. 1. It stood there unchallenged and uncertified by the plaintiff although. It is seen from the rent receipts that the defendant No. 1 always paid the rent for the whole property and there is nothing on record to show that the plaintiff ever paid rent for his own share and if defendant No. 1 and the plaintiffs were equal owners it is not understood as to why defendant No. 1 would be obliged to pay for the whole. It further appears that a portion of the partible land was acquired in L.A. case No. 2 of 1966 and it is seen that in that L.A case the compensation was assessed in the name of defendant No. 1 alone who withdrew the compensation money without any protest from the plaintiff. If the plaintiff was 8 annas shareholder of the property he would also be 8 annas owner of the compensation money and the entire amount could not be paid to one co-sharer without the authority of another. This clearly shows that the plaintiff was never a co-sharer to the extent of 8 annas share of the property as claimed. Those exhibits were documentary evidence and they would have been enough for a finding as to the alleged co-ownership of the property to the extent of 8 annas by the plaintiff which was the subject matter of the partition suit and the learned court of appeal below on a consideration of the testimony of both the P.Ws. and D.Ws. found those to be equal on both sides and hence it considered the documentary evidence as a corroborating evidence to lend support to the oral testimony of persons, who were considered by the Court to have special means of knowledge as members of the family or otherwise, to testify to the relationship of the plaintiff with Gour Majhi. Those statements found on various Government records as to distribution and devolution of the family property and as to ownership, was rightly considered by the Court of appeal below as a piece of evidence of family conduct under section 50 of the Evidence Act is pedigree as a relevant circumstantial evidence, corroborating the testimony of the witnesses.
